verses.text: Now concerning things sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
But if anyone thinks that he knows anything, he doesn’t yet know as he ought to know.
But if anyone loves God, the same is known by him.
Therefore concerning the eating of things sacrificed to idols, we know that no idol is anything in the world, and that there is no other God but one.
For though there are things that are called “gods”, whether in the heavens or on earth; as there are many “gods” and many “lords”;
yet to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we live through him.
However, that knowledge isn’t in all men. But some, with consciousness of the idol until now, eat as of a thing sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.
But food will not commend us to God. For neither, if we don’t eat, are we the worse; nor, if we eat, are we the better.
But be careful that by no means does this liberty of yours become a stumbling block to the weak.
For if a man sees you who have knowledge sitting in an idol’s temple, won’t his conscience, if he is weak, be emboldened to eat things sacrificed to idols?
And through your knowledge, he who is weak perishes, the brother for whose sake Christ died.
Thus, sinning against the brothers, and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
Therefore if food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat forever more, that I don’t cause my brother to stumble.

footnotes.content: Paul opens with a truth I had to learn the long way: knowing the right answer doesn't make us right. Knowledge alone puffs us up like yeast—gives us size but hollows us out. Love, though, builds up steadily, making us stronger where it counts, in our bonds with one another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: How humbling—and how true. I've met so many confident in their knowledge, yet blind to what they're blind to. The moment we think we've arrived at understanding is often the moment we've stopped listening. Real knowledge listens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But here's the flip side Paul sets in place: knowing *about* God is one thing; being *known by* God is another—that's what matters. It's not the size of my understanding that counts; it's whether I'm loved and seen by Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul grounds the Corinthian dilemma in a firm fact: an idol is nothing. No power there, no pollution in food. The meat is just meat. But this is where theology and real people collide—knowing this truth doesn't settle the whole matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The world is full of false gods—names, titles, powers people bow to—but Paul isn't speaking with scorn here. He's naming what is, plainly, so he can lead somewhere deeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This confession is the heartbeat of Paul's faith. One God, the Father—source of all. One Lord, Jesus Christ—through whom all things exist and we live. When you've said this truly, you've settled something deep: there is only one power that matters, and we belong to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's where theory meets a real human being. Someone in the congregation grew up seeing idols worshipped; the old worship clings to their conscience like a shadow. Knowledge of the truth doesn't instantly erase that wound. Paul sees that weaker conscience with compassion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What we eat or don't eat—it's neutral ground with God. The meal doesn't change our standing, doesn't open heaven or close us out. This freedom is real. But Paul is building toward something more important than my freedom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The turn. My liberty is true, but it's not mine to spend thoughtlessly. If my freedom becomes a trap for my brother—a stone he stumbles over—then I've used my gift against him. That's where Paul draws the line.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Picture it: a strong Christian sits down at a temple table, eating without hesitation. A weaker believer watches and feels the old lie whisper back: maybe this false god isn't so powerless after all. Conscience wars with what they see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the weight Paul lays on us: that believer who stumbles isn't just confused—he's a brother for whom Christ died. His soul cost the same blood as mine. When I wound his conscience through my liberty, I wound someone Jesus counted worthy of His life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul speaks with terrible clarity: when I harm my brother's conscience, I sin against Christ Himself. It's not a small thing, a private preference. It's a wound given to the One who loves us all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's answer—and his conviction—still echoes across the centuries: if food makes my brother stumble, I will not eat it. Period. Readers today hear an echo of the same challenge: what liberties will I lay down for love? Which hills am I willing not to die on?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
